title: Online participation is becoming more passive while confidence, critical ability, safety, and well-being diverge
source_unit: Ofcom, Adults' Media Use and Attitudes 2026
geography: United Kingdom adults aged 16 and over, with age, gender, socioeconomic, and online-use comparisons

denominator.unit: UK adults aged 16+ in the Adults' Media Literacy Tracker survey

overall_confidence.unit: percent reporting high overall confidence online

sponsored_result_accuracy.unit: percent of search-engine users correctly identifying sponsored results in a test

fake_profile_accuracy.unit: percent of social-media users correctly identifying a fake profile

observations.method: Ofcom quantitative media-literacy survey with scenario tests, supplemented by Adults Media Lives qualitative context.
observations.uncertainty: Survey confidence and scenario performance are not equivalent to real-world behavior, and test performance does not establish vulnerability to all forms of manipulation, fraud, or misinformation.
observations.subgroup: UK adults by age, gender, socioeconomic group, breadth of online use, and confidence in specific digital skills.
observations.counterinterpretation: High confidence can support experimentation and agency, while imperfect test performance may reflect unfamiliar scenarios rather than persistent inability.

denominator.unit: UK online adults in Ofcom social-media behavior comparisons

active_participation.unit: percent sharing, posting, or commenting on social media in 2026

active_baseline.unit: percent sharing, posting, or commenting in 2024

new_site_exploration.unit: percent using lots of new websites in 2026, down from 24 percent

read_only.unit: percent mainly reading without much interaction

observations.method: Ofcom survey measures of UK online behavior and longitudinal qualitative media-life context.
observations.uncertainty: The report notes methodological changes affecting trend interpretation; posting and commenting do not capture private messaging, offline action, or the quality of participation.
observations.subgroup: Younger and older adults, active and passive users, socioeconomic groups, and people using social media for communication, video, information, or recommendations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower public posting can reflect healthier boundaries, privacy preferences, or a shift toward private and small-group communication rather than disengagement.

observations.period: 2026; online well-being, screen time, and perceived risk

denominator.unit: UK online adults and social-media users in Ofcom attitudes measures

benefit_risk_balance.unit: percent saying the benefits of being online outweigh the risks

mental_health_benefit.unit: percent of social-media users saying platforms are good for their mental health

screen_time.unit: percent saying they sometimes spend too long on screens

frequent_screen_time.unit: percent saying this happens most days

observations.method: Ofcom survey measures of online benefits, risks, social-media attitudes, screen-time concerns, and perceived online behavior.
observations.uncertainty: These are perceptions and self-reports; they do not establish clinical mental-health effects, addiction, or a causal effect of platform design on time use.
observations.subgroup: Social-media users, younger adults, women, people with negative online experiences, and users with different activity patterns.
observations.counterinterpretation: The same online environment can support learning, connection, creativity, government access, and skill-building while also generating overload or harm concerns.

observations.period: 2026; digital exclusion and unequal meaningful participation

denominator.unit: UK adult population and online-user access frame

home_offline.unit: percent of adults without internet access at home

smartphone_only.unit: percent of online adults relying solely on a smartphone for access

narrow_users.unit: percent of users classified as narrow internet users

concentration.value: offline and narrow-use groups are disproportionately older, female, and in lower socioeconomic households

observations.method: Ofcom access, device, skills, confidence, and online-use analysis in the 2026 adult media-literacy report.
observations.uncertainty: Access and use categories do not measure the quality, affordability, privacy, reliability, or social value of connectivity for each person.
observations.subgroup: Older adults, women, lower socioeconomic households, people with limited digital confidence, and users dependent on a single device.
observations.counterinterpretation: Smartphone-only access can be functional and empowering for some uses, while broader device and skills access may still matter for work, public services, and complex tasks.

related_sources.claim: Ofcom Online Nation context on platform time, AI search, children’s online activity, online spending, and action after harmful content.
Ofcom 2026 news-consumption context on intermediaries, social platforms, video, and AI tools.

boundary: This record adds a UK platform-attention, media-literacy, online-well-being, and digital-inclusion route. It reports aggregate publication findings and test summaries; it is not respondent-level analysis, behavioral telemetry, a clinical mental-health study, or a causal estimate of platform effects.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Ofcom Adults' Media Use and Attitudes 2026 report and related Ofcom online-habits context were reviewed; confidence, scenario performance, participation, well-being, screen-time, and digital-inclusion claims were cross-checked.
